platforms.title: Your Constant Fatigue Might Be an Underactive Thyroid
platforms.meta_description: Feeling tired all the time and gaining weight isn't always just aging. How to tell simple fatigue apart from hypothyroidism, and how a blood test settles it.
platforms.body_html:
Sleeping enough but still exhausted, and gaining weight without eating any more than usual? It's easy to chalk that up to age or stress, but the American Thyroid Association points out that an underactive thyroid can be the real cause. Unlike simple fatigue, this comes from the small, butterfly-shaped gland in the front of your neck not producing enough hormone.

Why fatigue and weight gain show up together

Thyroid hormone controls the body's metabolic rate — how fast it burns energy. With hypothyroidism, that hormone runs low, so metabolism slows down across the whole body, and fatigue, weight gain, feeling unusually cold, constipation, dry skin, and thinning hair often show up together as a cluster. The most common cause is Hashimoto's disease, an autoimmune condition.

According to the American Thyroid Association, the biggest risk factors are being female, a family history, having another autoimmune condition, being over 60, and the period right after giving birth. If any of those apply alongside unexplained fatigue and weight changes, it's worth not writing it off as just being tired.

How to tell it apart from simple fatigue, and how to check

First, fatigue that doesn't lift even with enough sleep and rest, showing up alongside weight gain, feeling cold, or constipation. Ordinary tiredness from not sleeping enough usually clears up with rest, but fatigue from an underactive thyroid tends to stick around no matter how much you sleep.

Second, these symptoms building up gradually but steadily over months, several at once. That overlapping cluster is what sets it apart from an ordinary rough patch.

If those signs show up, a simple blood test called TSH can confirm it. It's not a complicated test, so it's far faster to get it checked than to keep guessing based on symptoms alone. Once diagnosed, hypothyroidism is usually managed with one thyroid hormone pill a day, and since the right dose varies from person to person, follow-up blood tests fine-tune it over time.

What makes this tricky is that every one of these symptoms overlaps with plenty of other, more common explanations — poor sleep, low iron, depression, or just a demanding season of life can all produce similar fatigue and mood changes on their own. That overlap is exactly why guessing at home isn't reliable in either direction: it's easy to blame a real thyroid problem on stress for months, and just as easy to fixate on the thyroid when something else entirely is going on. A blood test settles the question either way instead of leaving it as a guess, without needing to wait months to see whether things eventually improve or simply keep getting slowly and steadily worse on their own regardless, week after week without fail.

The takeaway: ongoing fatigue paired with weight gain, feeling cold, or constipation is worth checking with a thyroid test rather than blaming it on age or stress. This article is for general health information; consult a medical professional for diagnosis and treatment.
